title: Impermanent Loss Lab
objectives: Understand why providing liquidity costs you when the two tokens diverge
Know the market conditions where fees actually beat the loss

steps.title: The Hidden Cost of Providing Liquidity
steps.body:
Two friends agree to share a fruit basket that must always hold equal value in apples and oranges. The moment apples get expensive, the basket quietly sells apples and buys oranges to stay balanced. That rebalancer is your <Term id="amm">AMM</Term>.

Deposit 50/50 into a <Term id="liquidity_pool">liquidity pool</Term> — SOL and USDC, say — and arbitrageurs trade against it as the market price moves.

When SOL doubles in price:

- The pool sells your SOL into the market on the way up and collects USDC in return.
- You exit holding less SOL and more USDC than if you had simply left both tokens in your wallet.

That gap is <Term id="impermanent_loss">impermanent loss</Term>. The sting is that the pool did nothing wrong — it did exactly what it was designed to do. The arbitrageur's profit came out of your position. You are not being hacked; you are paying for a mechanism that always sells the winner and buys the loser.

The fees your <Term id="lp_token">LP tokens</Term> collect are the compensation for accepting that trade-off.

steps.title: The Mathematical Reality of IL
steps.body:
The cost of divergence follows one formula. For a price ratio `r = P_new / P_old`, your loss relative to simply holding is:

`IL = 2 × sqrt(r) / (1 + r) - 1`

The table worth memorising:

- 1.25x price change: about -0.6% IL
- 1.50x price change: about -2.0% IL
- 2.00x price change: about -5.7% IL
- 5.00x price change: about -25.5% IL

Three things to notice:

- Small moves barely hurt. Under a 2x divergence the damage stays in single digits.
- The loss is symmetric. A 0.5x crash costs about the same as a 2x pump, because the formula only cares about the ratio, not the direction.
- It is only 'impermanent' while the ratio can still return to 1.0. Withdraw while prices are diverged and the loss becomes real.

That last point is the whole game. Impermanent loss is a paper wound that heals only if you wait for the two prices to meet again.

steps.title: Under the Hood: Fees vs. Impermanent Loss
steps.body:
Being a profitable liquidity provider comes down to one inequality: `Trading Fees Earned > Impermanent Loss`. Everything else is commentary.

Where each side comes from:

- Fees grow with swap volume. Busy pools churn constantly, so this side fills fast.
- Impermanent loss grows with divergence. Sideways action keeps it near zero; a one-way trend inflates it steadily.
- Pool depth matters on both counts. Thin pools suffer larger <Term id="price_impact">price impact</Term>, which shows up to traders as <Term id="slippage">slippage</Term> and quietly makes the pool less attractive to trade against.

When each side usually wins:

- High-volume, range-bound markets let fees outrun the loss, so the position grows.
- Violent one-way trends do the opposite. The pool keeps selling the runner or catching the faller, and the loss can devour a large slice of your capital.

The practical read is that providing liquidity is not free yield. It is a bet that fee income will beat divergence — a bet won or lost almost entirely by how choppy versus how trending the market turns out to be.

questions.prompt: Why is the divergence cost suffered by liquidity providers called *impermanent* loss?
options: Because the blockchain rolls the loss back if you file a complaint within 24 hours
Because it only exists on test networks and never touches real capital
Because if the price ratio returns to its starting level before you withdraw, the loss versus holding disappears
Because the protocol refunds part of it through emissions each epoch
questions.explainRight: The gap is measured against holding, and it closes to zero if the two prices drift back to their original ratio before you exit. The name is a reminder that the loss only locks in when you withdraw.
questions.explainWrong: No chain reverses a trade because you complained, and this is not a testnet quirk. The loss is called impermanent because it vanishes if the ratio returns to its starting point. Exit while prices are still diverged and it lands in your wallet for good.

questions.prompt: In a standard 50/50 pool, SOL doubles in price relative to USDC (r = 2). Roughly how much impermanent loss does the LP suffer versus simply holding both tokens?
options: About -50%
About -5.7%
0%, because the pool automatically rebalances back to even
About -100%
questions.explainRight: Plug r = 2 into the formula: 2·sqrt(2)/(1+2) − 1 ≈ −5.7%. It is a surprisingly small number for a doubling, which is exactly why fees can often cover it. The position still gains value; it just trails a plain hold.
questions.explainWrong: A 2x divergence does not cost half your capital and does not zero it out. Rebalancing is real — it is the mechanism that creates the shortfall in the first place, not the thing that erases it.

questions.prompt: Impermanent loss is always measured as a difference between two specific things. Which two?
options: The pool's fee income versus the pool's gas costs
The value of the LP position versus the value of simply holding the same tokens in a wallet
The token price today versus the token price exactly one year ago
The LP token supply versus the protocol's total token emissions
questions.explainRight: It is a relative measure: what your pooled position is worth versus what those same tokens would be worth if you had just held them. That HODL comparison is the yardstick the formula expresses in one variable, the ratio r.
questions.explainWrong: Impermanent loss is not about gas, price charts, or token supply. It compares two portfolios at the same instant — your share of the pool versus holding the same tokens yourself.

questions.prompt: Using IL = 2·sqrt(r)/(1+r) - 1, what is the impermanent loss when one token rises 4x relative to the other (r = 4)?
options: About -20%
About -4%
About -50%
About -40%
questions.explainRight: sqrt(4) = 2, so 2·2/5 − 1 = −0.2, or about −20%. Notice how disproportionately the loss grows: doubling the divergence from 2x to 4x more than triples the shortfall. It accelerates as the ratio drifts from 1.
questions.explainWrong: Work the formula directly — −20%, not −40%. The tempting −40% assumes the loss scales linearly with the price move, but it is convex and grows faster than that.

questions.prompt: A liquidity provider ends up profitable overall only when which condition holds?
options: Trading fees earned, plus any reward emissions, exceed the impermanent loss suffered
The two tokens in the pool hold exactly the same price forever
The LP withdraws before a 24-hour protocol fee lock expires
The pool's TVL grows faster than the token's market cap
questions.explainRight: The entire LP business model is that one inequality. Fees and emissions are the income; the loss is the cost of always selling the winner and buying the loser. When income outpaces the cost the position grows, and when divergence wins it shrinks.
questions.explainWrong: There is no 24-hour fee lock, and prices never need to sit still. What decides it is whether accumulated fees and reward emissions outrun the divergence cost.

questions.prompt: Which market condition is generally the friendliest to a liquidity provider?
options: A strong one-way trend where one token rises relentlessly
A strong one-way crash where one token falls relentlessly
High swap volume with the two tokens trading sideways, so fees accrue while the ratio stays near 1
A quiet period with almost no trading, so the pool stops rebalancing
questions.explainRight: LPs want lots of fees with little divergence, and range-bound markets with heavy volume deliver exactly that. Plenty of swaps push income into the reserves while the ratio hovers near 1, keeping the loss near zero.
questions.explainWrong: One-way trends, up or down, push the ratio far from 1 and inflate the loss. A dead-quiet pool is nearly as bad because it collects almost no fees. The sweet spot is high volume with sideways prices.

questions.prompt: You deposit $1,000 as 50% SOL / 50% USDC into a pool. SOL then rises 4x in price. Ignoring fees, roughly what is your LP position worth versus the $2,500 you would have if you had simply held the tokens?
options: About $2,000, because the pool sold much of your SOL on the way up - roughly a 20% gap versus holding
About $2,500, identical to holding because no tokens were ever lost
About $1,250, because the pool gives away half of any gain by design
About $3,000, because AMMs amplify gains on the winning token
questions.explainRight: A plain hold gives $2,000 of SOL plus $500 of USDC, so $2,500. The pool kept selling SOL as it climbed, so its value is $2,500 × 0.8 = $2,000. That ~$500 gap is the loss — real money left on the table relative to HODL.
questions.explainWrong: Price the hold path first: $500 of SOL becomes $2,000 at 4x, plus $500 of USDC is $2,500. The pool cannot match it because it sold into strength the whole way up. AMMs do not amplify gains; against a strong trend they lag a plain hold.
